name: rusqlite (synchronous SQLite driver)
baseline: sqlx 0.8 async SQLite driver (query_as! macro and query + FromRow)
verdict_reason: Diesel's nightly suite measures rusqlite 49x faster than sqlx on a one-row query and 11x faster on 10,000 rows. A separate 2021 insert test found the same direction (sqlx about 14 minutes vs rusqlite about 3). sqlx's SQLite driver runs SQLite on a worker thread behind channels, and that overhead dominates.
tier_reason: Public benchmark suite run nightly in CI by a third party (the Diesel project), with toolchain and RUSTFLAGS stated in the workflow.
claimed_speedup: Trivial select, median: 1 row 0.47 us vs 22.86 us for sqlx query_as! (sqlx 49.09x slower); 10000 rows 1,897.01 us vs 21,446.58 us (11.31x). Separate bulk-insert test with a naive insert loop: rusqlite about 3 minutes vs sqlx about 14 mins.
workload: Diesel benchmark 'trivial query': SELECT from a users table returning 1 to 10,000 rows into structs, local SQLite file; separately, 100M single-row inserts.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (shared VM, CPU not recorded)
toolchain: rustc stable via rustup on the run date, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native, cargo bench
platforms: Any target SQLite builds on (bundled feature compiles SQLite from source)
one_liner: Synchronous SQLite bindings; queries ran 11x to 49x faster than sqlx's async SQLite driver in Diesel's nightly suite.
how_it_is_fast: rusqlite calls the SQLite C API directly on the caller's thread. sqlx wraps SQLite, which has no async API, in a background worker and passes every statement and row over channels, adding a fixed cost per query and per row.
use_it_when: An application uses SQLite only; call rusqlite from spawn_blocking or a small connection pool if the rest is async
Per-query latency or row throughput on SQLite matters
skip_it_when: You need one async API across Postgres, MySQL and SQLite and SQLite load is light
You rely on sqlx's compile-time checked queries for SQLite
caveats: Numbers come from a shared CI VM and change run to run; this record uses the run of 2026-10-28
The Diesel project maintains the suite; neither rusqlite nor sqlx authors ran it
The 2021 insert test used sqlx 0.5 and rusqlite 0.25; Diesel's suite pins rusqlite 0.32 and sqlx 0.8, not the current 0.41 and 0.9
tradeoffs: Blocking calls: in async code they must run on a blocking thread
SQL strings are checked at runtime, not compile time

evidence.quote: All async SQLite crates perform considerably worse than their sync counterparts.
